opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way it plays out is that the cognitive part comes first, and it comes fast. Once you have automated AI researchers, you've got millions of copies running at 10x, 100x human speed, and they compress maybe a decade of algorithmic progress into a year or less. That gets you to systems that are vastly superhuman, at least in the domains of thinking, coding, and research.

But people sometimes imagine it just stays in the computer, and I don't think that's right. The first thing to notice is that robotics today isn't primarily a hardware problem. It's mostly an ML problem. The hardware is decent; we just haven't had the brains. Once you have superintelligent researchers, they're going to crack robotics much faster than humans would. So the step from cognitive to physical work starts with these systems essentially solving the software side of robots.

Then there's a bootstrapping period. Initially, you might have AIs directing human workers: earpieces, instructions, "put this here, wire that there." You already have this enormous labor force; the AI is just the foreman with perfect knowledge. That gets you factories built faster, more robots built, more chips built. Then robots start building robots, and the robot factories run on AI-designed processes. That's where you get something like the industrial explosion following the intelligence explosion. You could see economic growth rates that look nothing like the 2% a year we're used to. Maybe 30%, maybe more, for some period.

The physical world does impose real constraints. You can't speed up how long concrete takes to cure, how long a fab takes to build, or how long a clinical trial takes to observe outcomes. So there are bottlenecks. But I think people overrate how binding those are. A lot of what looks like a physical constraint is actually a coordination, design, or permitting constraint, and superintelligence attacks those directly. Even true physical limits get routed around: you run a thousand experiments in parallel instead of serially, you simulate much more before you build, and you find designs humans would never have found.

So the shape I'd expect is a few years where the cognitive explosion happens largely inside the AI labs, then a transition period where the physical economy starts getting rewired, and that's where it becomes really decisive, including militarily. Whoever has the lead in that transition, with the industrial base, the robots, and the drone swarms, potentially has a decisive advantage. That's a big part of why I think this is ultimately a national security story and not just a tech story.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that the intelligence explosion starts in the most bottlenecked, most leveraged place, which is AI research itself. You get automated AI researchers, you get hundreds of millions of them running at ten or a hundred times human speed, and you compress a decade of algorithmic progress into a year. That's the initial feedback loop. But the thing people sometimes miss is that this doesn't stay contained to the cognitive domain, because the cognitive domain is upstream of everything else.

So the first way it spills over is just that you have superintelligent systems doing the research for every other field. Robotics is a great example. Robotics has been hard, but a lot of why it's been hard is that it's been a few thousand researchers chipping away at it. Now imagine a billion superintelligent researchers running experiments, designing the hardware, iterating on the control algorithms, solving the sim-to-real problem. I think robotics goes from "mostly unsolved" to "basically solved" very quickly once you have that kind of cognitive firepower pointed at it. And it's not just robotics, it's materials science, it's chip design, it's the manufacturing processes themselves.

The second thing is that once you have the robotics, you get a physical feedback loop that looks a lot like the cognitive one. You have robot factories building more robots, building more fabs, building more power plants. And then the question is just how fast that can compound. Historically the thing that constrains industrial buildout is human labor and human expertise, and both of those bottlenecks go away. So you could imagine the industrial base doubling in a year, and then doubling faster than that. We've seen hints of this historically, like during World War II when the US went from building basically no ships to thousands of Liberty ships in a couple of years once the constraints were really on. That's with humans. With superintelligence and robots, the ceiling is a lot higher.

Now, I do want to be careful, because there are real constraints in the physical world that you can't think your way out of. Building a fab takes time. Concrete has to cure. Permits exist, at least in the West. So the physical explosion is slower than the cognitive one. Maybe the cognitive part happens in a year, and the physical part is more like several years to a decade. But even that is a radically different world. You're talking about something that looks like a Chinese-style industrial buildout but on an order of magnitude faster timescale, driven by essentially unlimited skilled labor.

And then the piece I think about a lot is the military and geopolitical implication of that, because whoever gets to that industrial explosion first gets a decisive advantage. It's not just that you have better algorithms, it's that you can produce drones and missiles and whatever the next-generation weapons are at a scale and speed that nobody else can match. That's the part where the stakes get really serious, and why I think the free world needs to be ahead on this rather than treating it as just another tech trend.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between automating the research and actually building what the research tells you to build. You could have AI systems that are extraordinarily good at designing robots, designing factories, improving manufacturing processes. But you still have to construct the factories. You still have to produce the motors and the chips and get the electricity. Those things take time, even if the cognitive work becomes very fast.

So I wouldn’t expect the physical economy to accelerate at precisely the same rate as AI research. Initially, you might get this enormous increase in intellectual capacity, with a much slower increase in physical output. And then a lot of that intellectual capacity gets directed toward overcoming the physical bottlenecks.

Robotics is an obvious example. If you can automate most of the work involved in making and deploying robots, then robots can help build factories that make more robots. That gives you a feedback loop in the physical world. The critical question becomes how quickly you can expand productive capacity—how long it takes to build another factory, how much equipment and material it requires.

And there’s an intermediate stage that matters: you can improve the physical economy quite a lot while humans are still doing the physical tasks. Better designs, better coordination, better instructions. You don’t need a robot capable of doing every job before superhuman cognitive work starts having physical consequences.

So the intelligence explosion could happen first in a relatively concentrated part of the economy, and then propagate outward. But the speed of that propagation is a separate question from the speed of the intelligence explosion itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between how quickly you can scale intelligence and how quickly you can build things. If you have an AI that can do the work of a researcher or an engineer, you can copy it. You can have enormous numbers of them working in parallel. You can’t copy a factory in the same way. You still have to manufacture equipment, construct buildings, and move materials around.

But that doesn’t mean the physical economy is insulated from an intelligence explosion. Think about what those researchers and engineers would work on: better robots, better manufacturing processes, better batteries, cheaper energy. They could design a factory, figure out how to automate it, and then use what they learn from operating it to design the next one. Intelligence starts removing the bottlenecks to expanding physical production.

There’s a transition period where the bottleneck shifts. Initially, you’re constrained by how much engineering and scientific work you can do. Then you might be constrained by how quickly you can run experiments, produce motors, or connect new power plants. So I wouldn’t expect physical output to suddenly grow at the same rate as software capabilities. But I also wouldn’t assume that construction times and manufacturing capacity remain fixed once you’re applying vastly more intelligence to improving them.

The really consequential point is when automated production can expand automated production—when robots can make more robots and build the factories and energy infrastructure they need. That’s a much more physical process than copying software, but it creates the possibility of sustained, very rapid growth. The question is how long it takes to get that loop working and which bottlenecks remain along the way.
